source.title: Characterizing signal propagation to close the performance gap in unnormalized ResNets
source.authors: Andrew Brock; Soham De; Samuel L. Smith

record.tranche_reason: The study compares training speed and stability of normalizer-free and batch-normalized residual networks, bearing on V6's normalizer-free residual-network clause with a different method.
record.gate_note: The study reports no CIFAR training-error results. ImageNet accuracy tables report test accuracy, so those values do not measure the claim's training-error outcome. Training-throughput comparisons and the explicit RN288 collapse result bear on V6's normalizer-free speed and stability clause. Signal-propagation plots are initialization diagnostics, not trained classification-error results.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares stable learning rates for FixUp, SkipInit and batch-normalized ResNets, and reports stability of another normalization-free recipe. These results bear on V6. Iterations per second measure computational throughput, not how quickly networks learn.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that signal scaling and Scaled Weight Standardization enable normalization-free residual networks with stable training, low training losses and competitive ImageNet test accuracy. Their reported speed advantage is computational throughput, not demonstrated faster convergence. Stability remains dependent on depth, learning rate, regularization and architectural choices.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a normalizer-free residual-network recipe using signal scaling and Scaled Weight Standardization, with SkipInit in the ResNet experiments; it compares against batch-normalized networks and FixUp/SkipInit baselines rather than reproducing V6's cited methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth and regularization affect stability: some unregularized 288-layer NF-ResNets collapse at learning rate 0.4; reducing the rate to 0.2 removes instability but costs test accuracy. Training throughput varies by depth and batch size; some entries are OOM.

fits_no_version.finding: NF-ResNets execute more training iterations per second than BN-ResNets in the readable Table 4 comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing activation normalization with this replacement recipe can improve computational throughput on a single 16GB V100.

record.problems: Training error is not numerically reported; the paper gives only qualitative statements about higher training accuracies and low training losses. Throughput comparisons are iterations per second rather than accuracy-versus-time, and the 288-layer unregularized result reports successful-run statistics after two runs collapsed.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Test-accuracy tables and signal-propagation plots were not extracted as training-error results; the former measure test accuracy and the latter are initialization diagnostics.

untested.parts: CIFAR training classification error, random labels, and size or training-duration effects.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization and extra student neurons.
Plain-versus-residual depth degradation and the specified plain-tanh and Fixup exceptions.

Initialization effects on learning speed and trainable depth in plain networks; orthogonal-versus-Gaussian comparisons. The signal-propagation experiments use residual networks and do not establish these outcomes.
Initial linearized stability limits, catapult recovery, and edge-of-stability sharpness trajectories.
Accuracy-versus-time or iteration learning curves establishing equal learning speed; the original sigmoid, VGG and Inception settings. No numerical maximum stable learning-rate sweep is supplied.

missing.what: FixUp and SkipInit required peak learning rate 0.2 for stable training, while BN-ResNets used 0.4; the shared schedule uses five-epoch warmup and 90 epochs at batch size 1024.
Stable training at peak learning rate 0.4 for regularized NF-ResNets across 50–288 layers, contrasted with collapse only in the deepest setting without added regularization.

The linear learning-rate/batch-size relationship breaks down beyond batch size 1024 for unnormalized ResNets, versus 2048 or 4096 for normalized ResNets; optimal and highest stable learning rates decrease at larger batches.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for any listed version. Test accuracy alone does not establish training-error or learning-speed claims. NF-ResNets use a different recipe from FixUp, so their failures should not be attributed to FixUp.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, corrupted or random labels, and model size or training duration effects.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and student width relative to teacher width.
No plain network without identity shortcuts is compared with a matched residual network; the reported depth sweep uses residual networks.
No comparison of the specified activation-matched, orthogonal, or Gaussian initializations for plain networks or trainable depth.
No above-stability-limit learning-rate mechanism or sharpness trajectory is tested.

The study measures training throughput in iterations per second, not accuracy gained over training time, and does not compare tolerance to higher learning rates between matched normalized and unnormalized models across settings.
